Comparative evaluation of large language model chatbots for pheochromocytoma education: accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability.
desc: [Frontiers in public health] Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly used for medical information, but their suitability for pheochromocytoma education remains uncertain. We compared four contemporary LLMs for knowledge accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability. ChatGPT (ChatGPT-5.6 Sol), DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V4 Flash), Gemini (Gemini-3.6 Flash), and Grok (Grok-4.5 Fast) answered 200 pheochromocytoma-related multiple-choice questions across three independent trials. Google Trends and clinician input were used to develop 15 patient-centered questions. Responses were evaluated using DISCERN, EQIP, GQS, JAMA benchmark criteria, and six readability indices. Overall knowledge accuracy differed among the four models (p = 0.0012), with mean accuracy rates of 93.00% for ChatGPT, 91.17% for DeepSeek, 90.50% for Gemini, and 81.67% for Grok. However, after adjustment for multiple comparisons, statistically significant pairwise differences were limited to ChatGPT versus Grok for overall accuracy (adjusted p = 0.0129) and clinical-presentation questions (adjusted p = 0.0088). No significant differences were identified among ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini. Exploratory assessments of 15 patient-oriented questions suggested differences in information quality, transparency, and readability across models. ChatGPT showed comparatively favorable information quality scores, whereas DeepSeek exhibited a more favorable descriptive readability profile. Nevertheless, transparency was limited across all models, and none achieved the recommended sixth-grade readability standard. The evaluated LLM-based chatbots demonstrated generally favorable performance on structured pheochromocytoma-related knowledge questions, although statistically significant pairwise differences in accuracy were limited. Findings from the exploratory patient-oriented assessments suggested potential differences in information quality and readability but require confirmation in larger studies. Persistent limitations in transparency and readability highlight the importance of clinician oversight, source verification, and linguistic simplification before these tools are used for patient education.

title: FairMed-XGB: A Bayesian-Optimised Multi-Metric Framework with Explainability for Demographic Equity in Critical Healthcare Data
desc: Background:Machine learning models in emergency medicine often exhibit demographic biases, particularly gender disparities, which can compromise fairness, clinical trust, and decision-making reliability. Existing mitigation approaches typically optimise isolated fairness metrics, failing to address the multi-dimensional nature of bias while maintaining predictive performance and interpretability. Methods: We propose FairMed-XGB, a Bayesian-optimised, multi-metric fairness framework integrated into an XGBoost classifier. The model incorporates a composite fairness-aware loss function combining Statistical Parity Difference, Theil Index, and Wasserstein Distance. Bayesian optimisation is used to balance fairness and predictive accuracy. The framework is evaluated on seven cohorts derived from the MIMIC-IV-ED and eICU datasets. SHAP-based explainability is employed to analyse feature contri

title: CellTouch: Learning to separate touching nuclei in anisotropic 3D cell cultures
desc: 3D-oids, such as spheroids and organoids, are essential models in drug discovery and precision medicine, and quantitative analysis requires every nucleus to be segmented separately. Accurate 3D instance segmentation remains challenging, because nuclei are densely packed and touching, and volumes are sampled more coarsely along the Z-axis than laterally. Most existing methods were developed for near-isotropic data and tend to merge neighbouring nuclei. To address this challenge, we propose CellTouch, a deep learning method for anisotropic 3D nuclei instance segmentation that predicts flow fields and a contact channel, which separates touching nuclei directly from the network output. Ablations showed that the contact channel is the key design element, and CellTouch outperformed state-of-the-art methods on in-house data and widely used public datasets. Most importantly, dense Z-sampling is not required: CellTouch segmented nuclei as accurately at a 2 um Z-step as at 0.5 um, reducing acquisition time and data volume four-fold.

title: Preoperative Prediction of Vessels Encapsulating Tumor Clusters Status in Hepatocellular Carcinoma by Integrating Multiphase Contrast-Enhanced MRI Intratumoral Habitat Radiomics, Deep Learning, and Clinical Features.
desc: [Journal of hepatocellular carcinoma] To develop and evaluate a Combined model integrating multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI intratumoral habitat radiomics, deep learning, and clinical information for preoperative, noninvasive prediction of vessels encapsulating tumor clusters (VETC) status in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). A total of 140 patients from two centers were pooled and randomly divided at the patient level into a training cohort (n=98) and an internal hold-out test cohort (n=42); no independent center-level external validation was performed. MRI sequence-specific k-means clustering was performed separately on arterial-phase, portal venous-phase, and delayed-phase images to generate three intratumoral habitats per phase. From each habitat, 107 radiomics features were extracted; the ITHScore model was developed after rank-sum testing, correlation filtering, and elastic-net selection. The DeepScore model was based on a ResNet-50 pretrained on RadImageNet. Peripheral washout, serum albumin, absolute lymphocyte count, ITHScore, and DeepScore were integrated into the Combined model. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration curves, calibration intercepts and slopes, Brier scores, decision curve analysis, DeLong tests, and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analysis. The Combined model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.885 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.819-0.950), a sensitivity of 0.857, and a specificity of 0.810 in the training cohort, and an AUC of 0.840 (95% CI, 0.711-0.969), a sensitivity of 0.824, and a specificity of 0.760 in the test cohort. In the test cohort, the AUCs of the Clinical, DeepScore, and ITHScore models were 0.631, 0.782, and 0.795, respectively. The Brier scores of the Combined model were 0.149 and 0.175 in the training and test cohorts, respectively. SHAP analysis identified ITHScore and DeepScore as the two largest contributors to the Combined model. The Combined model integrating multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI intratumoral habitat radiomics, a deep learning score, and clinical variables showed an AUC of 0.840 for identifying VETC-positive HCC in the internal hold-out test cohort and provided incremental value over the Clinical model alone. Independent external validation remains necessary.

title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
desc: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an op

title: L++: A Language for Programming Life
desc: Living systems run on a code written in DNA or RNA, but expressing that code as a model that scientists can write, run and read remains difficult. We present L++, a holistic programming language in which life can be described, simulated and, beyond that, designed; its nouns are biological, and people and AI systems can both write it. Molecules, reactions, compartments, cells, organs and populations are written directly and nest by containment, so one grammar spans a reaction and the population around it. Quantities carry units, objects take places in space, and values can be set in time. Named kinetic parameters select one family of rate laws, from mass action to cooperative enzyme kinetics, and a few operators write complexes, states and gene products in one line. Modules compose by import, and a process can be written by its inputs, outputs and rate before its mechanism is known; the aim is that one description can model an organism or design one. lppc compiles a program and lpps runs it, and a run repeats exactly with the same build, options and seed. Ten programs written with an AI assistant, from an enzyme in a tube to a lake ecosystem and a drug therapy from molecule to patient, show the language across levels of biological organization, and a genome-scale virtual Escherichia coli, reported separately, shows it holds a whole organism. Our ultimate goal is the Human Code: the human, from molecules to the whole body, written in L++ as a mechanistic model that runs.

title: Quality, Reliability, and Readability of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Information on Peri-Implant Diseases: A Comparative Study.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: The increasing use of dental implants has been accompanied by a rise in peri-implant diseases. As artificial intelligence (AI)-based chatbots are increasingly used to obtain health information, this study evaluated the reliability, quality, usefulness, and readability of responses generated by ChatGPT (GPT-4), Copilot (Smart GPT-5), and Gemini (3.0 Flash) to questions about peri-implant diseases. Methods: Thirty-two AI-generated patient-oriented questions about peri-implant diseases were submitted to each chatbot. The responses were evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS), a 4-point usefulness scale, the modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) tool, the Flesch Reading Ease (FRE), and the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Inter-rater agreement before consensus was assessed using single-measure, absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Statistical analyses included the Shapiro-Wilk, Kruskal-Wallis, post hoc Bonferroni, and Spearman correlation tests. Results: ChatGPT and Gemini had higher FRE scores and lower FKGL scores than Copilot (all adjusted p < 0.001). Copilot and Gemini had higher mDISCERN scores than ChatGPT (both adjusted p < 0.001), with no significant difference between Copilot and Gemini (adjusted p = 0.129). GQS and usefulness scores did not differ significantly across chatbots. Across the three chatbots, Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from -0.973 to -0.844 for the correlation between FRE and FKGL scores and from -0.773 to -0.509 for the correlation between GQS and usefulness scores. Conclusions: ChatGPT and Gemini produced easier-to-read responses than Copilot, while Copilot and Gemini scored higher than ChatGPT on mDISCERN. The chatbots showed no significant differences in overall quality or usefulness scores. Given their potential limitations in clinical depth, AI-generated responses should be used only as supplementary educational resources and should not replace professional medical advice.

title: ReviewSense: Cluster-Guided Evidence Selection for Actionable Review-to-Advice Generation
desc: Customer reviews are a rich but weakly structured source of operational feedback. We study ReviewSense, a cluster-guided evidence-selection workflow that converts review corpora into action-oriented advice for human decision support. Reviews are embedded with a sentence transformer, grouped by iterative cosine-similarity clustering with threshold decay, and reduced to compact evidence before Large Language Model (LLM) generation. Evaluating on dental and healthcare service reviews with expert judgment of actionability and annotator-based theme alignment, we find that a single central representative preserves the dominant cluster theme in 77.3% of cases but only 60.6% of secondary themes: central evidence captures main issues more reliably than minority concerns. Against fixed-generator LLM baselines, five cluster representatives yield the advice closest to expert recommendations while us

title: FunDLM: A Foundation DNA Language Model for Fungi
desc: Background: Fungi are important pathogens and biotechnology resources, but lack a broadly applicable fungal DNA language model. Models trained on diverse fungal genomes can support functional interpretation of genomic variants and a broad range of genomic tasks. Results: We introduce FunDLM, a family of four DNA language models pre-trained on 426 fungal reference assemblies spanning 217 genera and 14.3 Gb of sequence. Without task-specific training, FunDLM-Medium-1024bp distinguished phenotype-associated missense variants of Saccharomyces cerevisiae from synonymous controls with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.875. It performed comparably to Evo 2, a generalist model with about 15 times more parameters, and better than Nucleotide Transformer v3. The model also recognized mutations that disrupt start codons or introduce premature stop codons in S. cerevisiae and the blast fungus Pyricularia oryzae. Its scores for missense variants, computed from DNA alone, correlated with those of protein language models in S. cerevisiae and two Fusarium species (Pearson correlation 0.57-0.75). After fine-tuning, FunDLM-Small-1024bp identified supernumerary chromosome sequences in four Pyricularia isolates not used for training (average precision 0.884), and FunDLM-Medium-1024bp recognized centromeres on a chromosome withheld from training (AUROC 0.908). Fine-tuned models also predicted three histone modifications in an isolate and on chromosomes not used for training (AUROC 0.910-0.996). Conclusions: FunDLM provides reusable sequence representations for assessing functional impacts of fungal variants as well as annotation of genomic and epigenomic features. The released models, data, code, and benchmarks support applications across fungal species.

title: Fibromyalgia and the Gut Microbiome: Current Evidence, Mechanistic Insights, and Research Priorities.
desc: [Microorganisms] Fibromyalgia (FM) is a chronic condition characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, frequently accompanied by fatigue, sleep disturbances, and cognitive dysfunction. Studies have identified differences in gut microbial composition and metabolite profiles in some FM cohorts, but their consistency, clinical significance, and causal direction remain uncertain. This critical narrative review evaluates human observational evidence, experimental models, and microbiome-targeted interventions, distinguishing findings directly relevant to FM from mechanistic insights derived from other conditions. Particular attention is given to short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan metabolism, and bile acids as potential mediators of host-microbiome interactions along the gut-brain axis. Human studies are limited by small, predominantly female cohorts, inconsistent findings, and confounding related to gastrointestinal conditions, diet, medication use, and intestinal transit. Although transfer of FM-associated microbiota can induce pain-related phenotypes in experimental animals, these findings do not establish disease causation in humans. Evidence for dietary interventions, probiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation remains preliminary, with unresolved questions concerning efficacy, safety, and durability. We also propose a hypothetical framework of overlapping immune, metabolic, and neuroendocrine or stress-related domains to guide future investigation, not to define validated FM endotypes. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence (AI) may help test these hypotheses, but clinical applications require longitudinal research, independent validation, and adequately controlled trials.

title: AMIF: Authorizable Medical Image Fusion Model with Built-in Authentication
desc: Multimodal medical image fusion integrates complementary anatomical and functional information from different imaging modalities, providing richer image representations for clinical interpretation and assisted diagnosis. High-performance medical image fusion models are typically built upon medical images with high data sensitivity and security requirements, together with carefully designed algorithmic architectures. Collectively, these constitute intellectual property of significant value. As fusion results are circulated and reused in scenarios such as cross-institutional collaboration, traceable copyright protection and controlled authorization for these medical fusion assets are becoming increasingly important. However, existing multimodal medical image fusion models typically generate unprotected results and lack built-in copyright protection and authorization mechanisms. Conventiona

title: Extracting generator-specific information from irregular brain field potentials: a comparative study of feature-based and deep learning approaches.
desc: Brain field potentials (FPs) reflect the combined activity of multiple neural sources, challenging the accuracy of their temporal series and their spatial origin difficult to establish from waveform inspection alone. However, FP generators obtained by independent component analysis exhibit characteristic temporal patterns and unique spatial profiles that allow their identification, even during apparently irregular activity. Here, we compared feature-based machine learning (ML) and end-to-end deep learning (DL) approaches to assess how effectively this information can be extracted from short segments and whether learning directly from raw signals offers advantages over predefined signal descriptors. We analyzed irregular FP-generator activity from multiple hippocampal generators in a dataset pooled across experimenters, recording devices, and electrode types. Feature-based approaches used predefined spectral and nonlinear descriptors to construct multidimensional representations, which were classified using seven ML algorithms: bagged decision trees (BAG), light gradient boosting machine (LGBM), quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA), random forest (RF), support vector machines (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGB) and multilayer perceptron (MLP). In parallel, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer architectures learned discriminative representations directly from raw signals. Performance was evaluated using animal-independent data partitions to assess generalization to previously unseen animals. Both approaches discriminated among FP generators from short segments of irregular activity. Raw-signal models generally achieved higher classification performance than feature-based approaches, although the latter also captured substantial generator-specific information. This suggests that discriminative information extends beyond the predefined descriptors and includes temporal patterns that can be exploited through direct signal learning. Classification across animals further supports the reproducibility of generator-related information despite variability in experimental conditions and recording procedures. These findings provide a scalable quantitative approach to identifying FP generators from irregular activity, opening new possibilities for investigating electrophysiological signals across physiological and pathological conditions.

title: The Completion-Verification Gap in Clinical Nurses' Integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Into Nursing Work: A Qualitative Study.
desc: [Journal of clinical nursing] To explore how clinical nurses integrate generative artificial intelligence into nursing work, focusing on task support, perceived ability to verify outputs and professional responsibility. GenAI is increasingly used in nursing, but little is known about how nurses perceive their ability to verify outputs when task barriers are reduced, especially in evidence-sensitive or patient-related tasks. Between October and December 2025, a qualitative descriptive study was conducted in four tertiary hospitals in Nantong, China. Clinical nurses with experience of using GenAI were recruited using purposive maximum-variation sampling. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews and analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Data collection and analysis were conducted concurrently, with saturation assessed after 21 interviews and confirmed by one additional interview. Twenty-two clinical nurses were interviewed. Three themes and six subthemes were identified: (1) broadening GenAI use across nursing tasks, including progression from routine drafting to diverse nursing tasks and lowering task barriers; (2) the completion-verification gap, encompassing efficiency and learning support alongside superficial understanding and premature confidence; and (3) risk-calibrated integration, involving risk-based verification, retained professional responsibility and organisational safeguards. GenAI facilitated engagement with information-intensive and unfamiliar nursing tasks. However, easier task completion did not necessarily resolve perceived difficulties in identifying omissions, fabricated information or inappropriate recommendations. Safe integration therefore requires nurses to calibrate verification according to task risk, retain responsibility for final decisions and have access to organisational safeguards that support traceable and accountable use. Safe GenAI use in nursing requires risk-based verification, retained professional accountability and appropriate organisational safeguards. No patients or members of the public were involved because this study focused on clinical nurses' professional experiences.

title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
desc: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. title: Distance-stratified benchmarking of variant-effect predictors on β-lactamase deep mutational scanning data
desc: Mutations far from the active site of antibiotic-resistance enzymes can change resistance, but it is unclear what information predicts their effects. We asked how the performance of a protein language model (ESM2), a structure-based stability predictor (ThermoMPNN) and simple structural descriptors changes with distance from the catalytic residues, using deep mutational scanning data for the {beta}-lactamases TEM-1 (four assays) and VIM-2 (one assay). We measured Spearman correlation and AUROC within distance bins, with bootstrap intervals over positions. In TEM-1, ESM2 accuracy fell with distance (Stiffler assay: {rho} = 0.72 below 8 [A] and 0.42 beyond 20 [A]), while the stability score rose ({rho} = 0.41 to 0.70). Adding stability to a model of ESM2, solvent accessibility and neighbour count improved cross-validated {rho} by 0.02 below 8 [A] and 0.10 beyond 20 [A], and the combined model did not decline with distance. The pattern held across binning schemes, in a continuous-distance model, and when any one of five contiguous distal stretches was removed. Two TEM-1 assays are nearly duplicates, and the Deng assay was too noisy to be informative. VIM-2 has only seven positions beyond 20 [A] and showed no detectable trend within 20 [A], so it neither supports nor contradicts the TEM-1 pattern. Nine distal TEM-1 positions remained more sensitive than the models predicted. In TEM-1, predicted stability was more informative than the language model far from the catalytic site, and the language model was stronger near it. Distance-stratified reporting could add to variant-effect benchmarks. The study is exploratory and uses one structure and one phenotype per assay.

title: Metamaterial Absorbers Based on Deep Learning Inverse Design and MXene Ink.
desc: [ACS applied materials & interfaces] Traditional metamaterial absorber design suffers from reliance on manual experience, lengthy optimization cycles, and high computational costs. This paper proposes an intelligent method that integrates deep learning-based inverse design with MXene ink. First, by building a ternary MXene/PEDOT:PSS/CB conductive network, a functional ink was created that combines high conductivity with compatibility for screen printing, making high-precision manufacturing of complex metamaterial structures possible. Second, a dataset mapping structural topology to electromagnetic response was built through automated CST simulations, and a deep-learning surrogate model combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) attention mechanism was adopted. By extracting spatial topological features from the encoded metamaterial structure and using the SE module to amplify key feature channels, the model achieved high-precision electromagnetic response prediction (R2 = 0.93). Third, coupling this surrogate model with a genetic algorithm (GA) enabled automated inverse optimization, yielding an optimal structure with a -10 dB zero-order specular reflection band from 5.1 to 14.0 GHz and a minimum reflection loss of -20 dB. Experimental samples fabricated via screen printing demonstrated a measured -10 dB specular reflection band from 6.2 to 15.6 GHz, providing preliminary experimental validation of the proposed design strategy. Owing to this versatile design, our study offers a promising route for creating low-cost, high-performance electromagnetic absorbers.

title: Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios
desc: Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. title: Task-aligned foundation model representations enable single-cell cytokine response inference
desc: Inferring cellular responses from single-cell transcriptomes requires interpreting changes relative to an appropriate baseline while retaining cell-type context. Here we present CYTAP, which adapts frozen single-cell foundation model embeddings for cytokine-response inference by combining donor-adjusted receiver states with deviations from matched control centroids. CYTAP uses a shared classifier to assign relative single-cell response scores across 90 cytokines and supports unpaired analyses using counterfactual control references. Baseline-relative representations improved held-out-donor prediction with both State SE and scFoundation. Across independent perturbation datasets, CYTAP prioritized applied cytokines, including when receptor transcripts were sparsely detected, and ranked administered cytokines among the top ten in both in vivo datasets. In an unpaired COVID-19 cohort, inferred responses were associated with severity, and IL-6 response scores correlated with plasma IL-6 concentrations. These findings support the use of biologically defined references to adapt pretrained representations for functional response inference.

title: REFORGE: LLM-Assisted RTL Bug Repair with Structured Context and Verification Feedback
desc: Large language models (LLMs) can write and repair RTL, but successful compilation or testbench execution does not establish defect removal, behavioral preservation, security, or implementation feasibility. Existing LLM-based RTL repair methods often report a single repair rate without retaining separate evidence for these properties, limiting reproducible comparison and integration into hardware design flows. We present REFORGE, which, to our knowledge, is the first LLM-assisted RTL repair framework that maintains and accumulates structured repair evidence across iterations, allowing it to generate fixes that satisfy multiple objectives simultaneously, including functionality, behavioral equivalence, security, and cost efficiency. title: A Benchmark for Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Enzyme Kinetic Parameters of Metabolic Networks
desc: Large-scale kinetic models predict how metabolism responds to genetic and environmental perturbations, but building them at scale is limited by the scarcity of experimentally determined enzyme kinetic parameters. Generative machine learning has been proposed to address this bottleneck, yet prior work has each introduced a single, bespoke architecture, leaving open which generative paradigm suits this problem and why. We introduce a benchmark suite for generative modeling of high-dimensional enzyme kinetic parameter sets: labeled datasets of kinetically feasible Escherichia coli models paired with a mechanistically grounded evaluation harness that scores generated ensembles on dynamical stability and agreement with experimentally observed phenotypes, rather than statistical realism alone. Using it, we compare three standard architectures at matched capacity, a conditional variational autoencoder, a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty, and a RealNVP normalizing flow, each under two conditioning schemes (a discrete high/low label and a continuous, graded key-performance-indicator target), across a difficulty ladder from one mutant phenotype to a stringent class of nine reproduced jointly. Two findings stand out. The architectures trace a consistent concentration-exploration trade-off, the VAE concentrating, the flow exploring and extrapolating, the GAN in between, but this ordering is overturned at high stringency by the conditioning scheme: at the joint class, continuous targets reach 33 to 117-fold enrichment over random sampling for every architecture, whereas discrete labels stay at 1.3 to 15-fold. Beyond the comparison, the suite is an accessible, mechanistically validated reference task for groups outside the kinetic-modeling community to benchmark their own generative algorithms.

title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
desc: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together

title: rnaModScan: context-aware deep learning-based filtering of nanopore m6A and inosine calls
desc: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) can detect multiple RNA modifications, but falsepositive background calls complicate transcriptome-wide analysis. We developed rnaModScan,a deep learning filter that integrates Dorado scores for all eight modification types with local sequence, repeat, and per-read alignment features to distinguish N6-methyladenosine (m6A) and inosine candidates from background calls. Using public RNA004 data, we evaluated site classification by grouped five-fold cross-validation and assessed transfer to HeLa cellular RNA using model weights fitted exclusively to HEK293T cellular RNA and unmodified in vitrotranscribed controls. For m6A sites outside the canonical DRACH motif, filtering removed 92.85% of the Dorado/modkit candidates while retaining 93.34% of their original matches to the GLORI reference map. The F1 score relative to DRS-covered GLORI sites increased from 3.04% to 26.76%. For inosine, filtering removed 83.44% of the candidates while preserving 99.86% of their original Slic-seq matches, and the reference-map F1 score increased from 5.22% to 22.05%. Filtering also brought the motif, repeat, and transcript-position distributions of retained candidates closer to those in the orthogonal short-read maps generated by GLORI and Slic-seq. These results support rnaModScan as a practical complement to Dorado-based RNA004 analysis for prioritizing transcriptome-wide m6A and inosine candidates.Availability: rnaModScan is available at https://github.com/uedaLabR/rnaModScan and archived in Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24546829).Keywords: direct RNA sequencing; RNA modifications; Dorado; deep learning; inosine; m6A

title: Learning Image-based Tree Crown Segmentation from Enhanced Lidar-based Pseudo-labels
desc: Mapping individual tree crowns is essential for understanding and caring for our environment by improving the accuracy of urban tree inventories and precise monitoring of forest health. However, automatically separating tree crowns in aerial imagery is challenging because of factors like complex crown textures and frequent partial overlap between neighbouring trees. We present a method to train deep learning models to segment individual tree crowns from RGB and multispectral imagery, using pseudo-labels derived from aerial laser scanning (ALS) data. We show that incorporating information from a zero-shot instance segmentation model, Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2), improves model training. Our method enables training domain-specific optical image-based models without requiring manual training annotation. We trained and evaluated the models with data from an urban area in Southern Finlan

title: Confident but misplaced: a model-free ruler for post-translational modification placement by AI structure predictors
desc: AI structure predictors accept post-translationally modified (PTM) residues, but whether they place the added atoms where crystallography finds them, and whether their confidence reveals when they do not, is unknown. We first built a ruler from experiment alone: independent crystal structures of the same site reproduce the added atoms of oxidised cysteine and methionine to 0.32 [A], the closest pre-cutoff library rotamer lies at 0.41 [A] and a model-free guess at 4.17 [A]. We then predicted 176 hold-out PTM sites, released after every model's training cut-off, with RareFold, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and AlphaFold 3, using identical inputs and thresholds fixed before measurement. On oxidised Cys/Met (up to 34 sites in 25 proteins), the three all-atom models place the matching distal atoms of neighbouring canonical side chains to 0.35-0.38 [A] but the added oxygens at 1.19-1.51 [A]; 29-41 % of placements are wrong by more than 2 [A], as sterically plausible rotamers that the electron density does not support. RareFold misplaces ordinary side chains as well. Across all PTM classes, residue confidence does not flag the failure: at pLDDT [≥] 90, 24-46 % of modified-residue placements are catastrophic, 3.5-5 times the rate for matched canonical atoms. One seed rarely samples the correct rotamer; more seeds sample it more often, yet the models' own ranking does not select it. Methyllysine shows the same gap, whereas for pyridoxal-lysine the models diverge (AlphaFold 3 1.13 [A], Boltz-2 4.96 [A]). A high residue pLDDT at a modified residue therefore does not verify its side chain.

title: Beyond Anatomy: Interpreting Graph-Based ASD Classification Across ABIDE Settings
